catalog_quote: No words in Bakairi differentiate their meaning through the variation of stress. Indeed, stress is predictable in Bakairi. With very few exceptions, the main stress occurs on the second to last mora as illustrated below. [ˈnɨkɨ] 'he slept', [nɨˈkɨmɔ] 'they slept' ... [ˈeɣɔ] 'pestle', [eˈɡɔɾɯ] 'his pestle', [eɡɔˈɾɯmɔ] 'their pestle(s)' ... In monosyllabic words, the nucleus is realized as a long vowel. If we define a lengthened vowel as containing two moras, it may be stated that the minimal word in Bakairi is bimoraic. ... Words with four or more syllables can exhibit secondary stress on the second syllable to the left of the main stressed syllable. ... Rising diphthongs, as in CV.(C)GV##, fail to attract stress to the word-final syllable. Consequently, words ending in a rising diphthong do not constitute complex rhymes, as the glide [j] or [w] belongs to the syllable onset. In contrast…

audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-sensitive, right edge, stress on the penultimate mora with CVG falling diphthongs heavy) rests on a 2022 reference grammar with a dedicated stress section, held locally, and every quoted sentence in the record (quote, dq, exception footnote, nasal-suffix clause) was found verbatim at the stated sections/pages (2.4.1 pp.45-46; 2.2 p.35-36 region; fn.13). The 1892 von den Steinen statement (penult default, final stress on diphthong-final words) is also confirmed in the held scanned text at p.320 and independently agrees. Glottolog's bibliography and a Crossref sweep show no newer or more specialised stress/prosody study; the one open phonology article found (Rosa & Bonfim 2020) was fetched sources and is silent on stress placement; WALS has no stress coding for Bakairi. The two wishlist items (Wheatley's SIL phonemics ms., Meira 2005) are corroborative only and low priority.
